source.text: Papyrus Gets Vertical

translation.text: Papyrus 改用竖排

source.text: Papyrus' text box was ~ redesigned for the Japanese localization, although this made his Japanese font smaller than his English font

translation.text: 日语本地化重新设计了 Papyrus 的对话框，不过这也使他的日文字号比英文字号小。

source.text: Sans has a skeleton brother named Papyrus, whose name is also a reference to a cheesy, overused computer font. Papyrus' English text is unique in two ways: his dialogue uses the Papyrus computer font, and he only uses capital letters. This combination lends his dialogue a humorous "oddball" quality that no other characters in the game share.

translation.text: Sans 有个名叫 Papyrus 的骷髅兄弟，名字同样来自一种俗气、被用滥的电脑字体。Papyrus 的英文台词有两个特点：使用 Papyrus 字体，而且全是大写字母。这种组合给他的台词带来滑稽的“怪人”气质，游戏中其他角色都没有。

source.text: Like Comic Sans, the Papyrus font has a bad reputation for overuse and misuse

translation.text: 和 Comic Sans 一样，Papyrus 字体也因过度使用和滥用而声名狼藉。

source.text: Unfortunately, the Papyrus font doesn't support Japanese characters, nor does the Japanese language have capital letters. So, to ensure that Papyrus' text remained visually weird, funny, and memorable in Japanese, 8-4's technical team redesigned Papyrus' dialogue boxes to display text in Japanese tate style (vertically from top to bottom, moving right to left) instead of horizontally. The result is immediately striking and reinforces the idea that Papyrus is a happy go-lucky oddball who's oblivious to the world around him.

translation.text: 可惜 Papyrus 字体不支持日文，日语也没有大写字母。因此，为了让 Papyrus 的台词在日语中依然显得古怪、有趣、令人难忘，8-4 技术团队重新设计了他的对话框，采用日语 tate（竖排）形式：字由上往下，列由右往左，不再横排。效果立刻就很醒目，也进一步突出了 Papyrus 乐天、古怪、对周围世界浑然不觉的性格。

source.text: Almost every equipment ~ name ("Dusty Tutu" in this example) was too long to fit on one line in Papyrus' Japanese text box, so the programmers added a list of pre-formatted item names specifically for this one line of dialogue

translation.text: 几乎所有装备名称（此处为“Dusty Tutu”，沾灰的芭蕾裙）都太长，无法在 Papyrus 的日文对话框里放进一列。程序员因此专为这一句台词，新增了预先排好格式的物品名称表。

source.text: Because Undertale wasn't originally designed with vertical text in mind, Papyrus' Japanese text often led to graphical glitches and formatting problems. The localization team fixed this by manually editing all of Papyrus' text to use only five characters per line.

translation.text: Undertale 最初并未考虑竖排文字，因此 Papyrus 的日文台词经常出现显示异常和排版问题。本地化团队逐一手动编辑他的全部台词，把每列限制在五个字，解决了这些问题。

source.text: This solution wasn't perfect, though - in one scene, for example, Papyrus states the name of the main character's current equipment. Because most Japanese equipment names are longer than five characters, the equipment name would extend outside Papyrus' text window. The programmers fixed this rare issue by adding a new "Papyrus Equipment Name" list with pre-formatted equipment names.

translation.text: 但这个办法并不完美。例如某个场景中，Papyrus 会说出主角当前装备的名字。大多数日文装备名超过五个字，就会伸出他的对话框。程序员于是新增了一张“Papyrus 装备名称”表，存放预先排好格式的装备名，解决这个少见的问题。

source.text: All in all, it's clear that the localization team put serious effort into preserving Papyrus' Japanese dialogue, translation-wise and presentation-wise.

translation.text: 总之，本地化团队为了在日语中保留 Papyrus 台词的特色，无论翻译还是呈现方式，都下了很大功夫。

source.text: Naming Papyrus

translation.text: 给 Papyrus 起名字

source.text: LEFT: Papyrus was called タテルス ("Taterus") for a short time.

translation.text: 左：Papyrus 曾短暂地叫作“タテルス”（Taterus）。

source.text: RIGHT: "Taterus" was reverted much sooner than "Pop", but there was a short time when both names were in the Japanese script

translation.text: 右：“Taterus”比“Pop”更早被改回原名，但曾有一小段时间，这两个新名字同时出现在日文剧本中。

source.text: Because Papyrus' text uses the Papyrus font in the English version of Undertale, the localization team considered giving Papyrus a new name to match his new Japanese vertical text. Thus, for only a few weeks during the game's localization, Papyrus was known as "Taterus" - a combination of the Japanese word tate ("vertical") and "Papyrus". This name didn't last long, however, because it sounded too forced and not very funny.

translation.text: 由于英语版 Undertale 中 Papyrus 使用 Papyrus 字体，本地化团队考虑给他起个新名字，来配合日文的竖排台词。于是，在本地化过程中的短短几周里，Papyrus 被叫作“Taterus”：由日语 tate（竖向）与“Papyrus”组合而成。但这个名字听起来太牵强，也不太好笑，所以没用多久就放弃了。

source.text: Even after deciding to keep Papyrus' name as-is, the team faced a new issue: "papyrus" is a foreign word to begin with, so how should Papyrus' Japanese name be pronounced? Should it follow the English pronunciation or the Japanese pronunciation (roughly "pah pee roos")? The team chose the latter.

translation.text: 即使决定保留 Papyrus 的名字，团队仍遇到了一个新问题：“papyrus”（纸莎草）本来就是外来词，那么日语中这个名字该怎么念？是遵循英语发音，还是采用日语发音（大致是“pah pee roos”）？团队选择了后者。

source.text: Vertical Papyrus Reactions

translation.text: 玩家对 Papyrus 竖排台词的反应

source.text: In general, Japanese fans were delightfully surprised by Papyrus' new, vertical text style. Some on line responses to the initial reveal included:

translation.text: 总体而言，日本粉丝对 Papyrus 的新竖排台词感到惊喜。最初公布时，网上出现了这样的回应：

source.text: '' Papyrus is the only one with vertical text lo/

translation.text: 只有 Papyrus 是竖排，哈哈。

source.text: '' Papryus' vertical text is funny, but the smaller font lessens the impact. His insanely huge font made it sound like he was constantly shouting before.

translation.text: Papyrus 的竖排很好笑，但字变小了，冲击力也弱了。以前字号大得离谱，感觉他一直在吼。

source.text: '' His vertical text feels very "Japan"

translation.text: 他的竖排文字很有“日本”味。

source.text: '' Wow @Papyrus' text! It's so. .. avant-garde ... or perhaps classical?!

translation.text: 哇，Papyrus 的文字！真是……前卫……还是说古典？！

source.text: '' Papyrus' vertical text ... It's so adorable!

translation.text: Papyrus 的竖排……太可爱了！

source.text: '' Papyrus' dialogue is so hard to read now lo/! But I like him having vertical text

translation.text: Papyrus 的台词现在好难读，哈哈！不过我喜欢他用竖排。

source.text: '' Papyrus. .. Nay! He is now Taterus!

translation.text: Papyrus……不！现在该叫 Taterus 了！

source.text: '' I was worried Papyrus would end up sounding like an old-fashioned nerd, but after seeing this I can tell the official Japanese translation is really good

translation.text: 原本还担心 Papyrus 会变成说话老气的书呆子，看到这个之后，我知道官方日译真的很好。

source.text: '' I'm more shocked by Papyrus' vertical text than Sans' oira

translation.text: 比起 Sans 自称 oira（我），Papyrus 的竖排更让我震惊。

source.text: '' Wow. .. Papyrus' pronoun and speaking style were a surprise. It's a bit different from the unofficial translation, but charming in its own way

source.text: Papyrus Speaks

translation.text: Papyrus 的说话方式

source.text: Papyrus almost always uses the egotistical personal pronoun オレさま (ore-sama) in Japanese.

translation.text: 日语中，Papyrus 几乎总用自负的“オレさま”（ore-sama，本大爷）自称。

source.text: Papyrus is loud, delusional, and thinks very highly of himself. He even refers to himself as "the great Papyrus" in the English script on occasion. The translator replicated this character trait in Japanese by having Papyrus use similar speech patterns. This includes the use of the Japanese pronoun ore-sama, which is used by overly pompous characters with "I'm so great!" personalities.

translation.text: Papyrus 嗓门大、爱幻想，又特别自命不凡。英文剧本中，他有时甚至称自己为“伟大的 Papyrus”。译者让他在日语中使用类似的说话方式，重现这一性格，包括使用 ore-sama 这个自称：过分自大的、“我真了不起！”型角色就会这么说。

source.text: Papyrus uses the pronoun ボク (boku) in this rare scene in the Japanese script.

translation.text: 在这个少见的日文场景中，Papyrus 用“ボク”（boku，我）自称。

source.text: Papyrus always uses the pronoun ore-sama - except in one scene. If the player enters Sans' room, Papyrus will barge in to ask Sans about an action figure. In this one scene, when Papyrus thinks it's safe to be his true self, he refers to himself as boku. This detail adds charm to Papyrus' personality not present in the English line.

translation.text: Papyrus 总是自称 ore-sama，唯独一个场景例外。如果玩家进入 Sans 的房间，Papyrus 会闯进来，向 Sans 问起一个可动人偶。在这个场景里，Papyrus 觉得可以放心做真实的自己，便用 boku 自称。这个细节给他增添了英语台词中没有的可爱之处。

source.text: Papyrus Laughs

translation.text: Papyrus 的笑声

source.text: I would’ve transcribed Papyrus’ laugh as ニェヘヘヘ (roughly "nieheheheh") but that’s just how localization works - everyone makes different decisions.

translation.text: 我会把 Papyrus 的笑声写成“ニェヘヘヘ”（大致读作“nieheheheh”）。不过本地化就是这样，每个人都会作出不同选择。

source.text: Papyrus also has a unique laugh in English: "nyehehe". For reasons that are long forgotten, this was finalized as nyahaha in Japanese. It's possible that this was done because "nyehehe" can't be transcribed 100% perfectly into Japanese - any transcription would be an approximation at best. Whatever the case may be, Toby approved the choice of Papyrus' Japanese laugh.

translation.text: Papyrus 在英语中的笑声也很特别：“nyehehe”。日语最终定成了 nyahaha，当时的理由已经没人记得了。也许是因为“nyehehe”无法用日语百分之百准确地转写，再怎么写也只能近似。不论原因如何，Toby 认可了 Papyrus 日语笑声的这个选择。

source.text: Incidentally, because nya also happens to be the sound that cats make in Japanese, some Japanese fans have noted that Papyrus has a cat-like laugh that makes him sound cute.

translation.text: 顺带一提，日语里的 nya 正好也是猫叫声，因此有些日本粉丝觉得，Papyrus 的笑声像猫叫，听起来很可爱。

source.text: Ore is another common masculine pronoun in Japanese. It projects a sense of manliness, strength, confidence, being in charge, and/or vulgarity. As such, it's considered a bit crude, and isn't fit for formal situations or when trying to be polite. Among close friends and family, ore can instead indicate familiarity. Examples of fictional characters who use ore include:

source.text: Sibling Matters

translation.text: 兄弟姐妹的长幼

source.text: Papyrus refers to Sans as his 兄ちゃん (nīchan, "big brother") in Japanese.

translation.text: 日语中，Papyrus 称 Sans 为“兄ちゃん”（nīchan，哥哥）。

source.text: Sans and Papyrus are brothers, but which is the older brother and which is the younger brother? The English script leaves this unclear - they're simply brothers. What's more, Toby had intended for the brothers' relationship to remain unclear.

translation.text: Sans 和 Papyrus 是兄弟，但谁是哥哥、谁是弟弟？英文剧本没有说清，只知道他们是兄弟。而且 Toby 本来就打算让他们的长幼关系保持模糊。

source.text: Unfortunately, the brothers' uncertain relationship presented a major translation problem: there are words for "younger brother" and "older brother" in Japanese, but not for "brother" in general. Rather than make a blind guess, the translator consulted with Toby for details. Thus, through the translation process, it was definitively revealed that Sans is the older brother and Papyrus is the younger brother.

translation.text: 可惜，这种模糊关系造成了一个很大的翻译难题：日语有“弟弟”和“哥哥”的说法，却没有泛指单个“brother”的词。译者没有盲猜，而是向 Toby 询问详情。于是，通过翻译过程，Sans 是哥哥、Papyrus 是弟弟这件事才被明确揭晓。

source.text: The English script simply says "sister" here, while the Japanese script uses the word ねえさん (nēsan, "older sister").

translation.text: 这里英语只说“sister”（姐妹），日语则用“ねえさん”（nēsan，姐姐）。

source.text: This same relationship issue appeared elsewhere during Underta/e's Japanese localization. For example, a store owner mentions that she has a sister who manages the inn. In English, these two are simply referred to as sisters, but the Japanese language only has words for "younger sister" or "older sister".

translation.text: Undertale 的日语本地化中，其他地方也遇到了相同的亲属关系问题。例如，一位店主提到，她的姐妹经营着旅馆。英语只说明两人是姐妹，但日语需要区分“妹妹”或“姐姐”。

source.text: Again, the translator consulted with Toby to determine their relationship. Toby had never considered how these sisters relate age-wise, so he arbitrarily decided that the store owner is the younger sister and the innkeeper is the older sister.

translation.text: 译者再次询问 Toby，以确定她们的关系。Toby 从未想过这对姐妹谁大谁小，于是随意决定店主是妹妹，旅馆老板是姐姐。

source.text: In short, there are parts of the Japanese script that provide small details not present in the English script - not because anything was intentionally changed, but simply because of how the two languages work.

translation.text: 因此，日文剧本有些地方提供了英文剧本没有的小细节。这不是有人刻意改动了内容，只是两种语言的表达方式不同。

source.text: Sometimes things get lost in translation, but sometimes things become clear in translation too, as Undertale's Japanese localization demonstrates here.

translation.text: 翻译有时会丢失信息，但有时也会让事情变得清楚，Undertale 的日语本地化在这里就展现了后一种情况。

source.text: Dressing Up

translation.text: 盛装打扮

source.text: This text is unique to • the No Mercy route, incidentally

translation.text: 顺带一提，这段台词只在不留情路线中出现。

source.text: Papyrus is intent on making a name for himself by capturing a human. In one scene, he asks:

translation.text: Papyrus 一心想抓住一个人类，好让自己扬名。在一个场景中，他问道：

source.text: WHEN’S THE HUMAN SHOWING UP??? I WANT TO LOOK MY SUNDAY BEST... OR AT LEAST MY TUESDAY PRETTY-GOOD.

translation.text: 人类什么时候来？？？我要穿上我的 SUNDAY BEST（星期日的最佳盛装）……至少也得是 TUESDAY PRETTY-GOOD（星期二的还不错装）。

source.text: The English phrase "Sunday best" refers to the kind of nice, formal clothing one is expected to wear to church on Sundays. Only about 1% of the Japanese population is Christian, so a literal translation of "Sunday best" wouldn't make much sense, and the made-up "Tuesday pretty-good" would make even less sense.

translation.text: 英语短语“Sunday best”指的是星期日上教堂时应该穿的漂亮正装。日本人口中只有约1%是基督徒，因此直译“Sunday best”很难让人明白，自造的“Tuesday pretty-good”就更难懂了。

source.text: To work around this cultural barrier, the translator adjusted the line slightly:

translation.text: 为了绕过这道文化障碍，译者稍微调整了台词：

source.text: When's the human getting here? I need to dress in my yoso-iki [going somewhere formal] clothes ... or at least in my gokinjo-iki [going somewhere in the neighborhood] clothes!

translation.text: 日版大意是：人类什么时候来？我得穿上 yoso-iki（去正式场合）的衣服……至少也得是 gokinjo-iki（去附近串门）的衣服！

source.text: As we can see, the new Japanese text plays with the standard word yoso-iki by creating the made-up word gokinjo-iki. The end result is a Japanese joke that uses completely different wording to parallel the logic of the original English joke.

translation.text: 新版日语台词以现成词 yoso-iki 为基础，造出了 gokinjo-iki 来开玩笑。用词虽与原作完全不同，这个日语笑话却沿用了英语笑话的思路。

source.text: Apparently the phrase • "Sunday best" has been around since the 1600s - I wonder if we can get Toby's "Tuesday pretty good" to last for 400 years too

translation.text: 据说“Sunday best”从17世纪就有了。不知道能不能让 Toby 的“Tuesday pretty-good”也流传400年。

source.text: A localization team member explained the goal for Papyrus' text early on: "You can Google a lot of Papyrus's lines and he is the first search result because no one else has ever said anything like it. That's the kind of dialogue we should be striving for with him."

translation.text: 本地化团队的一位成员很早就解释过 Papyrus 台词的目标：“你把 Papyrus 的很多台词放到 Google 搜，第一条结果就是他，因为别人从没说过这种话。我们给他写台词，也应该追求这样的效果。”

source.text: Snowdrake Speaks

translation.text: Snowdrake 的说话方式

source.text: Snowdrake's new Japanese name suits him perfectly, although it does change him into a bird

translation.text: Snowdrake 的新日文名很适合他，尽管这也把他变成了一只鸟。

source.text: A young comedian monster named Snowdrake gets his name from the English words "snowflake" and "drake'', a type of dragon. Toby knew this wordplay might be tough to translate, so he left a note: "you can call him a bird if it makes it easier to make a pun [ ... ] the main thing about him is that he's a comedian".

translation.text: 年轻的喜剧演员怪物 Snowdrake，名字来自英语 snowflake（雪花）与 drake（一种龙）。Toby 知道这个文字游戏可能难译，所以留了条说明：“如果把他叫作鸟能更方便地造双关，就这么办吧［……］最重要的是，他是个喜剧演员。”

source.text: Based on Toby’s suggestion, the translator renamed the monster owaraichō, a combination of owarai ("comedy") and chō ("bird"). This name is also a play on the word raichō ("rock ptarmigan"), a bird associated with cold, snowy areas.

translation.text: 根据 Toby 的建议，译者把这个怪物改名为 owaraichō，由 owarai（搞笑）和 chō（鸟）组合而成。这个名字也玩了 raichō（雷鸟）的双关——这种鸟让人联想到寒冷、多雪的地区。

source.text: Raicho are iconic, culturally significant birds in Japan and are associated with deities, mountains, and snow

translation.text: raichō（雷鸟）在日本具有代表性和文化意义，人们把它与神明、山岳和白雪联系在一起。

source.text: In Japanese, Snowdrake speaks using a dialect associated with Osaka, the comedy capital of Japan. Snowdrake also uses the pronoun wate, which reinforces his connection to Osaka-style comedy.

translation.text: 日语中，Snowdrake 说的是大阪方言，大阪正是日本的喜剧之都。他还用 wate（我）自称，进一步强化了与大阪式喜剧的联系。

source.text: Japanese Personal Pronouns: wate

translation.text: 日语人称代词：wate

source.text: The pronoun wate is associated with people from the Osaka region. In entertainment, the Osaka dialect is associated with comedy, commerce, coarseness, and organized crime, among other things. Other fictional characters who use wate include:

translation.text: wate 这个自称让人想到大阪地区的人。在娱乐作品中，大阪方言常与喜剧、商业、粗豪和黑社会等联系在一起。其他使用 wate 的虚构角色包括：

source.text: The Japanese pronoun ワテ (wate) is less common in everyday Japanese these days, it’s another one that’s slowly fading away.

translation.text: 日语自称“ワテ”（wate）如今在日常生活中已不太常用，也是一个正在逐渐淡出的代词。

source.text: Icy What You Did

translation.text: Icy：看穿了你的把戏

source.text: Icecap’s Japanese name plays with the words 帽 (bō, "hat; cap") and 坊 (bō, "boy; lad").

translation.text: Icecap 的日文名利用了“帽”（bō，帽子）与“坊”（bō，小子）的同音。

source.text: A monster named "Icecap" sometimes appears in battle. He wears a hat made of ice that he considers his pride and joy. In Japanese, Icecap’s name became hyōbō - hyō means "ice", while bō is a play on the Japanese words for "cap" and "boy". This is an interesting, rare example of a name that works perfectly in a straightforward translation. Not only that, the Japanese name naturally contains an extra layer of wordplay not found in the English version.

translation.text: 战斗中有时会出现名叫“Icecap”的怪物。他戴着一顶冰做的帽子，对此引以为傲、爱不释手。日语中，Icecap 的名字变成了 hyōbō：hyō 是“冰”，bō 则同时指“帽子”和“小子”。这是个有趣而少见的例子，名字直译就能完美成立。不仅如此，日文名还自然地多出了一层英语版没有的双关。

source.text: Eye on Osaka

translation.text: 聚焦大阪

source.text: Osaka is the name of a major city and a prefecture in western Japan. The Osaka metropolitan area is the second largest in Japan, after Tokyo.

translation.text: 大阪是日本西部一座大城市及一个府的名称。大阪都市圈规模居日本第二，仅次于东京。

source.text: In broad terms, Japan can be divided into two cultural halves, with Osaka representing western Japan and Tokyo representing eastern Japan. This division includes language, too - the Japanese dialect associated with Osaka sounds significantly different from the more "standardized" Tokyo dialect.

translation.text: 大致而言，日本文化可分为东西两部分，大阪代表西日本，东京代表东日本。语言也有这样的区分：大阪方言与较为“标准化”的东京方言，听起来有明显差异。

source.text: 1. Osaka

translation.text: 1. 大阪

source.text: 2. Tokyo

translation.text: 2. 东京

source.text: Osaka Castle, first built in 1583, is one of Japan's most famous landmarks

translation.text: 大阪城始建于1583年，是日本最著名的地标之一。

source.text: Osaka is home to Dotonbori, a famous tourist destination and entertainment district

translation.text: 道顿堀位于大阪，是著名的旅游目的地和娱乐街区。

source.text: The city of Osaka is rich in culture and history. As a port city and a major financial center, Osaka is associated with commerce, merchants, and shipping. As the comedy capital of Japan, Osaka is where many comedians master their craft before breaking into the mainstream comedy circuit. Osaka is also famous for its food, and is sometimes referred to as "the nation's kitchen".

translation.text: 大阪有丰富的文化和历史。作为港口城市和重要金融中心，大阪让人联想到商业、商人与航运。它也是日本的喜剧之都，许多喜剧演员在这里磨炼技艺，再进入主流喜剧圈。大阪还以美食闻名，有时被称为“天下的厨房”。

source.text: Stop Right There

translation.text: 就地停下

source.text: In his translation notes, ~ Toby emphasized this gameplay hint is meant to sound "obtuse". Clarification is at the heart of translation, so I find that translating "obtuse" stuff can either be really fun or really nightmarish

translation.text: Toby 在翻译说明中强调，这条玩法提示应该显得“晦涩”。翻译的核心是把事情说清，所以在我看来，翻译这种“晦涩”内容，要么非常有趣，要么简直是噩梦。

source.text: Sans explains that a blue-colored attack in battle won't cause damage if the player remains still. He then suggests a needlessly complicated technique for remembering this fact:

translation.text: Sans 解释，战斗中的蓝色攻击不会伤害静止不动的玩家。然后，他提供了一个毫无必要地复杂的记忆方法：

source.text: imagine a stop sign. when you see a stop sign, you stop, right? stop signs are red. so imagine a blue stop sign. simple, right? when.fighting, think about blue stop signs.

translation.text: 想象一个停车标志。看到停车标志，你会停下，对吧？停车标志是红色的。那么，想象一个蓝色停车标志。简单吧？战斗时就想想蓝色停车标志。

source.text: Stop signs are red in Japan too, so this hint would be easy to translate into Japanese without any major issues. However, the translator felt the information would "click" more naturally in Japanese if it referred to a stoplight instead of a stop sign. Thus the line became:

translation.text: 日本的停车标志也是红色，因此这条提示直接翻成日语也不会有什么大问题。不过，译者觉得，用交通信号灯代替停车标志，日本玩家会更容易“明白过来”。于是台词变成了：

source.text: everyone stops when a stoplight turns red, right? red stoplights mean "stop", but think ofb lue as "stop", okay? simple, right? in battle, blue means "stop".

translation.text: 日版大意是：信号灯变红，大家就会停下，对吧？红灯表示“停”，不过把蓝色当成“停”，好吗？简单吧？战斗时，蓝色就表示“停”。

source.text: This new text doesn't really seem to be that different from the original text, but there's a cultural reason behind it: in Japanese, green stoplights are called blue stoplights. And since real-life "blue" stoplights and red stoplights are opposites, it makes sense for Sans to swap the two in his overly complicated explanation.

translation.text: 新台词乍看与原文没什么不同，但背后有一个文化原因：日语会把绿色交通灯叫作蓝灯。现实中的“蓝灯”与红灯意思相反，因此 Sans 在那番过分复杂的解释里把两者对调，就说得通了。

source.text: LEFT: English- ~ speaking players are asked to imagine this

translation.text: 左：英语玩家被要求想象这个。

source.text: RIGHT: Japanese players are asked to imagine this instead

translation.text: 右：日本玩家则要想象这个。

source.text: On a slightly different note, this whole blue/green issue is a common challenge when translating between Japanese and English. One time, I had to translate a Japanese anime script without any video to check, so I basically had to guess a color and hope it was right. Later, when I saw the final product, I was relieved to see that my guess was right.

translation.text: 稍微岔开一下，蓝色与绿色的区别是日英翻译中的常见难题。有一次，我翻译日本动画剧本时没有视频可核对，只能基本靠猜颜色，祈祷自己猜对。后来看到成片，发现没猜错，才松了口气。

source.text: Blue and Green in Japanese

translation.text: 日语中的蓝与绿

source.text: For linguistic and historical reasons, the Japanese word 青 (ao) usually means "blue" in English, but can instead mean "green" in some situations. In general, ao means "green" when referring to plants, fruits, vegetables, and other types of "vibrant" green. Ao can also mean "green" in relation to other things, including stoplights and being new to something.

translation.text: 由于语言和历史原因，日语“青”（ao）通常对应英语的“蓝”，有时却指“绿”，尤其用于植物、水果、蔬菜等鲜活的绿色。交通灯也用 ao，而“新手”、不熟练的意思也与英语 green 相通。

source.text: This sky is ao in Japanese

translation.text: 这片天空在日语中是 ao。

source.text: These chili peppers are also ao in Japanese

translation.text: 这些辣椒在日语中也是 ao。

source.text: Mega Mail

translation.text: 洛克人的战斗装甲

source.text: Game theory: does the Mega Man series exist in the Undertale universe?

translation.text: 游戏猜想：Undertale 的世界里也有 Mega Man 系列吗？

source.text: Sans shares inside information about Papyrus’ unusual clothing. In English, he says:

translation.text: Sans 透露了 Papyrus 那身奇特装束的内情。英语版中，他说：

source.text: we made that a few weeks ago for a costume party. he hasn't worn anything else since. .. keeps calling it his "battle body."

translation.text: 几周前，我们为了化装舞会做了这身衣服。从那以后，他就没换过……老管它叫自己的“battle body”（战斗躯体）。

source.text: Toby noted that the term "battle body" is a direct reference to Sigma’s "battle body" in Mega Man X3. The translator checked the original Japanese version of Mega Man X3, found that it used the term sentōyō bodi ("body for combat use"), and then used that term in the Japanese Undertale script.

translation.text: Toby 说，battle body（战斗躯体）直接引用了 Mega Man X3 中 Sigma 的称呼。译者查过日文原版，便把其中的 sentōyō bodi（战斗用躯体）用于 Undertale 日文剧本。

source.text: Toby borrowed the term "battle body" from Mega Man X3, but Papyrus' costume isn't based on Sigma's battle body

translation.text: Toby 从 Mega Man X3 借来了“battle body”这个词，但 Papyrus 的服装并不是照着 Sigma 的战斗躯体设计的。

source.text: This obscure reference is easy enough to miss in the English script. So without Toby's input, it probably would've been missed in translation too.

translation.text: 这个冷僻的梗在英文剧本中就很容易被忽略。若没有 Toby 的提醒，它大概也会在翻译中被漏掉。

translation.text: 雪镇

source.text: Searching for Words

translation.text: 寻找单词

source.text: Reader Challenge #3: ~ Solve both word searches and see how their solutions are different

translation.text: 读者挑战③：解开这两道寻词题，看看它们的答案有何不同。

source.text: Papyrus plants a trap to stall the main character's progress: a word search puzzle intended for children.

translation.text: Papyrus 布下陷阱，想拖住主角：一道给孩子玩的寻词题。

source.text: The English word search puzzle features one nonsense word and eleven normal words for the player to find. Some of the words are related to smoking because the puzzle's in-game creator loves to smoke.

translation.text: 英语寻词题里有一个无意义的词和十一个普通单词，供玩家寻找。其中几个词与吸烟有关，因为游戏中这道题的创作者很爱抽烟。

source.text: Just like the English word search, the Japanese word search features one nonsense word and eleven normal words as well. However, the Japanese word search has been resized and contains fewer total letters. Because of this, the English solutions and the Japanese solutions don't match.

translation.text: 和英语版一样，日语寻词题也有一个无意义的词和十一个普通词。不过，日语题目调整了尺寸，字符总数减少了。因此，英语版与日语版的答案位置并不相同。

source.text: Breaking the Ice

translation.text: 打破坚冰

source.text: The more I look, the ~ more it seems like the Duck Hunt dog's face is stuck on an ice cube

translation.text: 越看越觉得，这就像把 Duck Hunt 那只狗的脸贴到了冰块上。

source.text: In English, the word search puzzle is presented by a dog-faced ice cube mascot named "Ice-E", a play on the word "icy". A text bubble also includes a message from Ice-E:

translation.text: 英语版的寻词题由一个长着狗脸的冰块吉祥物介绍，名叫“Ice-E”，谐音 icy（冰冷的）。对话气泡里还有 Ice-E 的一句话：

source.text: Hey, kid's! Can you help me solve this puzzle?

translation.text:
Hey, kid’s! Can you help me solve this puzzle?
嘿，孩子们！能帮我解开这道题吗？

source.text: In Japanese, the mascot was renamed Burudokkun, which is also a play on words. Buru is the Japanese sound effect for shivering, the name ends with the friendly name suffix -kun, and the name resembles the word burudoggu, the Japanese word for "bulldog".

translation.text: 日语中，这个吉祥物改名为 Burudokkun，同样是文字游戏。buru 是日语的颤抖拟声词，名字末尾是亲切的称呼后缀 -kun，而且整个名字很像日语的 burudoggu（斗牛犬）。

source.text: Random trivia: there's a bulldog character in Shiren the Wanderer 4 (Nintendo DS, 2010) also called Burudokkun in Japanese, but it's just a coincidence

translation.text: 冷知识：Shiren the Wanderer 4（Nintendo DS，2010）里也有只斗牛犬，日文名同样叫 Burudokkun，不过只是巧合。

source.text: Ice-E’s Japanese text bubble closely matches what he says in English. It even emulates the "kid’s" apostrophe mistake in the English message by including a basic Japanese grammar mistake: using the character お (o) when を (o) should be used. With these two changes, the translator was able to keep the Japanese version of Ice-E an ice-themed mascot with an ice-themed name, saying something with bad grammar.

translation.text: Ice-E 日语气泡里的话与英语基本一致，甚至还用一个基础日语语法错误，重现了英语“kid’s”中多余的撇号：把本该用“を”（o，宾语助词）的地方写成了同音的“お”。通过这两处改动，译者让日语版的 Ice-E 仍然是个以冰为主题、名字带冰的梗、说话语法有错的吉祥物。

source.text: Crossing the Line

translation.text: 填字填出火气

source.text: In my experience, puns are generally easier to localize between Japanese and English when they involve a foreign loan word, such as in this scene

translation.text: 依我的经验，双关涉及外来词时，通常更容易在日英之间本地化，这个场景就是例子。

source.text: Papyrus shares his disgust for crossword puzzles by saying:

translation.text: Papyrus 这样表达了对纵横填字游戏的厌恶：

source.text: HMM. .. CROSSWORD. I GUESS IT'S AN APT NAME. THOSE WORDS MAKE ME CROSS!!!

translation.text: 嗯……CROSSWORD（纵横填字）。名字倒挺贴切。这些词让我 CROSS（生气）！！！

source.text: The English word "crossword" exists in the Japanese language, so the translator localized this pun by playing with the Japanese words kurosu ("cross") and kurōsuru ("to struggle with"). As a result, Papyrus now says in Japanese:

translation.text: 日语借用了 crossword，所以译者改用 kurosu（交叉）和 kurōsuru（苦恼、费劲）的近音作双关。日语台词变成：

source.text: HMM. .. CROSSWORD. .. THAT'S A GOOD NAME. BECAUSE I ESPECIALLY STRUGGLE WITH THEM! NYAHAHA!

translation.text: 嗯……纵横填字……这名字不错，因为我做起来特别费劲！NYAHAHA！

source.text: As we can see, the new Japanese line parallels the English line's tone and humor.

translation.text: 新的日语台词保留了英语台词的语气和幽默。

source.text: Jumbled Up

translation.text: 字母大乱斗

source.text: In a way, Junior Jumble seems fitting for skeletons, as they're basically a jumble of bones themselves

translation.text: 某种意义上，Junior Jumble（儿童乱字谜）倒挺适合骷髅，毕竟他们自己也就是一堆拼起来的骨头。

source.text: Sans and Papyrus argue about word puzzles. In English, Sans prefers crossword puzzles, while Papyrus prefers Junior Jumble, a real-life puzzle series aimed at children.

translation.text: Sans 和 Papyrus 争论起文字谜题。英语版中，Sans 偏爱纵横填字，Papyrus 则偏爱现实中面向儿童的谜题系列 Junior Jumble。

source.text: To make this reference work in Japanese, the translator replaced .Junior Jumble with Okosama Challenge ("Junior Challenge"), which is a parody of the real-life children's activity book Kodomo Challenge ("Child Challenge").

translation.text: 为了让日本玩家理解这个梗，译者把 Junior Jumble 换成了 Okosama Challenge（小朋友挑战），模仿现实中的儿童活动读物 Kodomo Challenge（儿童挑战）。

source.text: LEFT: Each Junior Jumble puzzle involves a clue, a drawing, and a word scramble

translation.text: 左：Junior Jumble 每题有提示、图画和字母重排。

source.text: RIGHT: Kodomo Challenge puzzles are designed as supplementary educational materials, but are easier than Junior Jumble puzzles

translation.text:
右：Kodomo Challenge
谜题用于辅助学习，
比 Junior Jumble 简单。

translation.text: 雪镇

source.text: A Link to the Past

translation.text: 连接过去

source.text: This is an interesting ~ example of how the solution to a localization problem is sometimes to change nothing at all!

translation.text: 这是个有趣的例子：有时解决本地化问题的办法，就是什么都不改！

source.text: A monster named Jerry is so annoying in battle that the player can team up with other enemies to "ditch" him. After several turns, however, Jerry will show up and annoy everyone again.

translation.text: Jerry 在战斗中太烦人，玩家甚至能和其他敌人联手“甩掉”他；可几回合后，他又会回来烦大家。

source.text: In the English script, Jerry's arrival is accompanied by the text "Return of Jerry". Toby noted that this is a reference to the classic 1988 game, Zelda II: The Adventure ofL ink. Specifically, it's a reference to the game over screen, which includes the text "RETURN OF GANON".

translation.text: Jerry 回来时，英文显示“Return of Jerry”（Jerry 归来）。Toby 说，这引用了1988年经典游戏 Zelda II: The Adventure of Link 的游戏结束提示：“RETURN OF GANON”（Ganon 归来）。

source.text: You know what, the ~ "Gannon" name should make a return someday, like maybe he'd be a copycat Ganon and the main villain in a spinoff game, but with everything slightly off about him

translation.text: 说真的，“Gannon”这个名字也该有一天重返舞台。比如做成一个山寨 Ganon，当外传游戏的大反派，不过浑身上下都微妙地不太对劲。

source.text: Zelda II game over screen (Japanese)

translation.text: Zelda II 游戏结束画面（日语版）

source.text: Zelda II game over screen (English)

translation.text: Zelda II 游戏结束画面（英语版）

source.text: The original Japanese version of Zelda II had a similar, English-language game over message: "RETURN OF GANNON". To retain this reference, the translator left "RETURN OF JERRY" entirely in English in the Japanese Underta/e script.

translation.text: Zelda II 的日文原版也有类似的英语游戏结束文字：“RETURN OF GANNON”。为保留这个梗，译者在 Undertale 日文剧本中完整保留了英语“RETURN OF JERRY”。

source.text: Jerry Speaks

translation.text: Jerry 的说话方式

source.text: The translator also had ~ to account for Jerry's unique text balloon, which appears above him and can't hold as much text as the standard text balloon

translation.text: 译者还得考虑 Jerry 特殊的对话气泡：它出现在头顶上，能容纳的文字比标准气泡少。

source.text: Toby designed Jerry to speak in an outdated and "irritating meme-y" way in English. To preserve this character trait in Japanese, the translator dropped all of the original English text and replaced it with roughly similar Japanese Internet slang that feels outdated and annoying. Jerry also tends to use the assertive and masculine Japanese pronoun ore.

translation.text: Toby 给 Jerry 设计的英语说话方式过时，而且“满嘴烦人的网络梗”。为了在日语中保留这种性格，译者放弃了原本的英文措辞，换成意思大致相近、同样过时又烦人的日语网络用语。Jerry 也常用强势、男性化的 ore（我）自称。

source.text: Waste Management

translation.text: 排泄与消灭

source.text: Without extra notes and context, I could absolutely see a rushed translator mistranslating this rarer usage of "eliminate"

translation.text: 如果没有额外说明和语境，我完全能想象，赶工的译者会误译 eliminate 这个较少见的用法。

source.text: Two married guard dogs block the way. The dogs can smell that a human is nearby, but can't quite find the source of the smell. The dogs, named Dogamy and Dogaressa, converse before battling the human:

translation.text: 一对结了婚的守卫犬挡住去路。它们闻到附近有人类，却找不准气味的来源。这两只狗叫 Dogamy 和 Dogaressa，在与人类开战之前，它们这样交谈：

source.text: Dogamy: Hmmm ... Here's that weird smell. Lt makes me want to eliminate.

translation.text: Dogamy：嗯……那股怪味在这儿。闻得我想 eliminate（排泄）。

source.text: Dogaressa: (...Eliminate YOU!)

translation.text: Dogaressa：（……eliminate YOU，消灭你！）

source.text: In English, the word "eliminate" usually means "to get rid of something" or even "to kill", but in some contexts - such as when discussing physiology or animal training- it can mean "to expel waste matter from the body". Toby made sure to mention this double meaning in his translation notes.

translation.text: 英语的 eliminate 通常表示“清除某物”，甚至“杀死”；但在某些语境中，例如讨论生理或动物训练时，也可以表示“把废物排出体外”。Toby 特意在翻译说明中提到了这层双重含义。

source.text: At first, the translator localized this wordplay by referring to bombs:

translation.text: 译者最初用“炸弹”来处理这个双关：

source.text: Do gamy: Here's the source of the smell. It makes me want to drop a "bomb".

translation.text: Dogamy：气味就是从这儿来的。闻得我想投一颗“炸弹”。

source.text: Dogaressa: ( ... We'll drop a "bomb" on you!)

translation.text: Dogaressa：（……把“炸弹”投到你身上！）

source.text: However, these "bomb" references didn't match the dogs' axe-themed attacks in battle, and they suggested that the dogs wanted to defecate on the main character. So the translator tried a different solution:

translation.text: 可是，“炸弹”与两只狗战斗中以斧头为主题的攻击不相符，还让人以为它们想往主角身上排便。因此译者换了一个办法：

source.text: Dogamy: Here's the source of the smell... It makes me want to "mark" it.

translation.text: Dogamy：气味就是从这儿来的……闻得我想“mark”（标记）一下。

source.text: Dogaressa: ( ..." Mark" you, that is!)

translation.text: Dogaressa：（……是把你“mark”为目标！）

source.text: As we can see, the word "eliminate" was simply replaced with the word "mark". In both English and in Japanese, the word "mark" can mean "to identify as a target" and, in the context of animals, "to mark one's territory with urine, feces, or other bodily substances". With this second localization solution, the translator was able to preserve the original joke in a way that avoided thematic conflicts.

translation.text: eliminate 就这样被换成了 mark。在英语和日语中，mark 都可以表示“确定为目标”；说到动物时，也能指“用尿液、粪便或其他身体物质标记领地”。第二种本地化方案让译者保住了原本的笑话，同时避免了主题上的冲突。

source.text: The English word "marking", as it relates to animal behavior, is already a part of the Japanese language

translation.text: 表示动物标记领地行为的英语词 marking，本身已经进入了日语。
